---
title: "Ship a pack in a Claude plugin"
---

A Claude plugin can carry a capt-hook pack, and dispatch discovers it: every
event, the dispatcher enumerates the project's enabled plugins and loads any
whose root ships a `[pack]` manifest. The pack applies to whatever project the
plugin is enabled in, with zero repo edits and zero per-session wiring — the
plugin runs nothing at all. This is the cc-context model.

The alternative is pinning the pack in a repo's committed
`.claude/capt-hook.toml`, so every clone hydrates the same commit — the
cc-notes model, right for a pack that encodes one repo's own conventions.
[Use packs](packs.qmd) covers that tier end to end; the rest of this page is
the plugin tier.

## The three artifacts

A pack plugin ships exactly three artifacts, and `pack lint` enforces exactly
these. There is no `hooks.json` involvement: the captain-hook plugin is the
sole dispatcher, and a plugin `hooks.json` that mentions `capt-hook` at all
predates this contract and fails lint.

**1. The pack manifest, `capt-hook.toml`.** A `[pack]` table at the plugin
root, or under a `hooks/` subdirectory — discovery probes both. Unchanged from
any other pack; [Author a pack](packs.qmd#author-a-pack) covers it.

**2. The dependency in `plugin.json`.**

```json
{
  "dependencies": [
    { "name": "captain-hook", "marketplace": "captain-hook", "version": ">=10.0.0" }
  ]
}
```

The object form is required: `name`, `marketplace`, and a version floor. A bare
`"captain-hook"` string, or an object missing the floor, fails `pack lint`.
Floor at `>=10.0.0` — the first release that discovers plugin packs. This
dependency is what pulls the dispatcher onto a machine that installs only your
plugin; without it the pack has no runtime at all.

**3. The allowlist in your marketplace's `marketplace.json`.**

```json
{
  "allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn": ["captain-hook"]
}
```

::: {.callout-warning title="The allowlist is load-bearing"}
Without this line, Claude Code skips a `plugin.json`-declared cross-marketplace
dependency at install — no error, no captain-hook, and every hook in the pack
stays dark. Verified on Claude Code 2.1.207.
:::

## Scaffold them

`pack scaffold` writes all three, plus a starter hook, and lints the result:

```bash
uvx capt-hook pack scaffold .
```

Pass the plugin root — the directory discovery probes for the manifest. In an
empty repo it creates every artifact; in a partial one it repairs in place,
adding only the missing contract pieces. It never touches content it can't
account for: a conforming file stays byte-for-byte identical, and an
unparseable one is reported and left alone. A plugin built against the old
attach contract migrates by deleting its capt-hook `hooks.json` line — scaffold
generates no `hooks.json` and lint fails any surviving `capt-hook` mention in
one. It closes by printing the two-line install snippet for your README.

## Tell users how to install

Two lines — your marketplace and your plugin:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add your-org/your-repo
claude plugin install your-plugin@your-marketplace
```

On a machine that has never seen captain-hook, installing just your plugin
surfaces Claude Code's dependency error: the `plugin.json` dependency points at
a marketplace the machine doesn't know, so the plugin lands disabled with
`dependency-unsatisfied`. The one-time fix is registering the marketplace —
`claude plugin marketplace add yasyf/captain-hook`, or `capt-hook init` in any
repo, which registers it as a side effect. From then on the dependency resolves
and Claude Code installs the dispatcher itself.

## How discovery works

Dispatch enumerates the project's enabled plugins via
`claude plugin list --json` and probes each one's install path — the root, then
`hooks/` — for a `[pack]` manifest. A plugin with no manifest merely consumes
packs and is skipped; a malformed manifest is skipped with a logged warning, so
one rotted plugin can't kill discovery.

That CLI spawns Node and takes about a second, far too slow for the ~3ms
dispatch hot path, so the roster is cached per project and invalidated by stat
changes to the files that shape it: Claude Code's `installed_plugins.json`, the
user, project, and local `settings.json`, and the `managed-settings.json`
locations (the config dir, `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/`, and
`/etc/claude-code/`). Installing, enabling, or disabling a plugin re-runs the
CLI once; every other event reads the snapshot. The manifest probe itself runs
live, so editing a hook file inside a plugin needs no invalidation at all. A
missing `claude` CLI, a failing invocation, or roster output in a shape
discovery can't use all degrade to an empty plugin roster — one warning, and
the empty roster is cached against the same stat tuple, so the failure never
becomes a per-event cost.

Two consequences of riding the plugin cache:

- Updates land on the next stat change. A plugin update moves its versioned
  install path and rewrites `installed_plugins.json`, so discovery picks up the
  new pack version on the next event. The session's *other* hooks are a
  different story: Claude Code keeps a running session on the old install path
  until `/reload-plugins` or the next session, so mid-session the pack and the
  plugin's own commands can briefly disagree on version.
- Dev plugins are untested. Discovery trusts whatever roster
  `claude plugin list --json` reports; whether a plugin loaded via
  `claude --plugin-dir` appears there is unverified. Lint and test the pack
  directly with `uvx capt-hook pack lint .` and
  `uvx capt-hook --hooks hooks test` instead of relying on discovery.

Discovered packs are first-class: they show in `uvx capt-hook pack list` as
kind `plugin`, and `uvx capt-hook test` loads and runs their inline tests
alongside everything else.

## Precedence

A `[packs.*]` entry in the project's `.claude/capt-hook.toml` always beats a
same-name plugin pack: a pinned external wins even while it is offline and
uncached, and a `disabled = true` entry suppresses the plugin pack outright.
That is the decline switch for a repo that wants none of an ambient plugin's
pack:

```toml
[packs.acme-notes]
disabled = true
```

Within the plugin tier, plugins resolve in stable plugin-id order. When two
plugins ship the same pack name, the lower plugin id wins and the clash is
logged at WARNING naming both — a genuine two-plugins-one-name conflict wants a
look, not a silent coin flip.

## Extra dependency marketplaces

captain-hook's own marketplace needs no declaration — wherever discovery runs,
the dispatcher already exists. If your pack's hooks depend on *other*
cross-marketplace plugins, list their `owner/repo` slugs in the `[pack]` table:

```toml
[pack]
name = "acme-notes"
description = "Note-taking guards"
hooks = "hooks"
marketplaces = ["yasyf/cc-present"]
```

Each slug is a plain `owner/repo` (no `github:` prefix); a malformed one fails
manifest load and therefore `pack lint`. When discovery resolves a pack
declaring an unregistered marketplace, it detaches a background worker that
runs `claude plugin marketplace add` for exactly the declared slugs. The spawn
prints nothing on either stream — dispatch stdout carries the hook decision —
and leaves only a log line plus the worker's own log as its trace. Claude Code
resolves the matching `plugin.json` dependencies from there and installs the
plugins. This works for every pack tier — a repo-scoped GitHub pack's
`marketplaces` declaration triggers the same worker.

The worker is damped: already-registered marketplaces short-circuit with a
single file read, a pack with no `marketplaces` costs zero I/O, and a failed
registration backs off for an hour per marketplace. See
[the troubleshooting entry](troubleshooting.qmd#discovery-installs-the-dependency-plugins)
for the worker's log.

Declare each extra in all three places: `marketplaces` here so discovery
registers the marketplace, a `dependencies` entry in `plugin.json` so Claude
Code installs the plugin, and its name in the `marketplace.json` allowlist so
the cross-marketplace dependency is permitted.

## Lint the contract

`pack lint` vets the three artifacts plus the pack itself and exits non-zero on
any failure, so CI needs one line:

```bash
uvx capt-hook pack lint .
```

Pass the plugin root — the same directory discovery probes. The checks:

| Check | Passes when |
|---|---|
| `manifest` | A `[pack]` manifest resolves under the root (or its `hooks/` subdirectory), with valid `marketplaces` slugs. |
| `hooks.json` | Absent, or free of the string `capt-hook` entirely — a raw-text scan, not a command parse. Any surviving attach or `run` line predates the discovery contract and fails; the migration is to delete it. |
| `plugin.json` | The captain-hook dependency is an object with `marketplace` and a version floor. |
| `marketplace.json` | `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn` includes `captain-hook`. A plugin with no `marketplace.json` upward gets a warning, not a failure. |
| `load` | The pack loads at least one hook with no load errors. Zero hooks fails — a pack that loads nothing ships no working guard. |
| `async-decision` | No hook registers `async_=True` on a decision-capable event — a background hook's verdict is discarded. Registration also raises on this at runtime. |

Packs may subscribe to `SessionStart`: discovery happens inside every event's
dispatch, so there is no registration-ordering race to guard against.

## Migrating an attach-era plugin

Releases before 10.0.0 wired plugin packs through a `pack attach` line in the
plugin's `hooks.json`. That command no longer exists. A plugin still shipping
the line triggers a non-blocking SessionStart hook warning in Claude Code — the
failed command is cosmetic, and the pack loads via discovery regardless. Ship a
cleanup release that deletes the attach line and floors the dependency at
`>=10.0.0`; `pack lint` confirms the result.
